cells.tense: The practice is running under its own weight right now, with the pen.
cells.ask: Pick one session this week and stop it early, on purpose, while it still feels good.
cells.core:
You're in a stretch where the work holds you instead of the other way around. Attention goes in and something comes back — the repetition is doing its quiet building, and you're not white-knuckling any of it. You sit down alone and it connects you to what you're making, rather than cutting you off from the day.

What fits where you are is what the practice lets end. You put the time in, something finishes, and you don't have to shove everything along by hand. Keep it steady by leaving one rep unfinished this week — the practice doesn't need the last ounce, it needs you back tomorrow.
cells.sheetLine: The practice holds you now, and you can let it.
cells.verb: keeping a small steady practice lit by attention
cells.place: a clearing where what was must end

cells.tense: Somewhere ahead is a version where this is finally finished, and you're already standing there.
cells.ask: End one session while it's still imperfect and let the imperfection stay overnight.
cells.core:
You're treating the work like a door you can close, and every session is another try at closing it. Perfect it, refine it, run it again — and somewhere in there the practicing stopped being something you do and became something you owe.

The time alone is where you keep pushing, because no one sees the gap between what you made and what you meant. That's the cost: the thing you're refining was supposed to feed you, and it's eating the hours instead.

What's finished and what's still open — one of those can be allowed to stay undone. Stop tonight at imperfect and leave it there until morning. Whatever settles when you loosen the grip is what the grip was doing, not what holds you up.
cells.sheetLine: You're refining like a punishment, not a practice.

cells.tense: Practice went somewhere it stopped being easy to keep, and you're still standing at that door.
cells.ask: Do the smallest possible version of the practice today, badly, and let that count.
cells.core:
Sustaining anything that asks for repetition has been hard, so the practice doesn't start — or it starts and quietly stops, in a pattern old enough that you mostly don't notice it happening. The skill is there. The keeping-at-it isn't, yet.

That isn't laziness. Steady effort has ended badly enough times that your shoulders brace before the first step, even where the details have gone. Gritting through won't help. Make the effort small enough that the bracing has nothing to push against, and let it be uneven.

Do a five-minute version today and let it be sloppy. Same tomorrow, or don't. The streak isn't the point — that trying became ordinary again is. Days you skip are neutral, not evidence.
cells.sheetLine: You can start badly. It still counts as starting.

cells.tense: The pen is moving in a room you'd say you just wandered into.
cells.ask: Catch one thing you're good at and say out loud, once, that you made it.
cells.core:
The skill gets described like something that arrived on its own — you happened to be there, it just works now, no big deal. But the sessions happened. The reps happened. Somewhere along the way, the refining got done, and the story drops that part out.

The ending you're in the middle of runs on the same missing piece: something is falling away, and it gets called circumstance instead of a room you cleared yourself. Same motion to say it — you kept showing up, and that's why it works.

Pick one thing you're good at and say, to yourself or someone else, that you made it. Not how. Just that. Then the ending will look less like something happening to you.
cells.sheetLine: You built this. You're clearing the room yourself.

attempts.check: The draft leans on 'a room where it didn't go well' for Too Little, which the record does not support — it only says past experience made practice feel dangerous, never what happened, who, or how long ago. A reader could reasonably say the solitude is chosen, not a hiding; the Balanced core honors that, and the Too Much core leaves room to disagree. The asks survive a wrong read because each one is a small testable move, not a verdict: doing the session badly, letting one thing lapse, naming one faith already kept, writing an unfinished sentence all teach the person something either way. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person was the too-tidy cause in Too Little, so it is narrowed to the mechanism and nothing behind it.
